quote: Sorry. Did you fill out a solar form online? This is Bucky with ION Solar.
stewart_read: The rep leads with a question about the form rather than a clean company/reason-for-call statement, and only supplies the company name after the customer's confused 'Excuse me?'. This delays the 'is this a scam?' answer the intro is supposed to front-load.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to lead every call with name + company + reason for calling before asking the customer anything, so legitimacy lands in the first line, not as a repair.

quote: So we have teams, like, everywhere. Like, personally, I'm located in, Utah because I'm in a like, I call. But there's our main team we have main teams in, like, Virginia, Illinois, South Carolina, just, like, everywhere.
stewart_read: The rep's answer to a simple location question is filled with filler and hedges ('like', 'I call', trailing clauses), which undercuts the confident, neighbor-like tone the schema calls for and does not actually answer where the customer's install would be handled from.
coaching_implication: Replay this clip with the rep — a direct, confident one-line answer here would have preserved credibility instead of sounding uncertain about his own company's structure.

quote: No. It negates my, it negates my metal roof warranty if I put it on my home.
stewart_read: This is a hard boundary about her existing metal roof, not a soft objection to overcome — the customer has ruled out rooftop solar entirely and wants a detached-structure option instead. The rep should investigate what would need to be true (a built pavilion) rather than probe the roof warranty claim itself.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep should have pushed back on the warranty claim; rejected because pursuing it would be arguing a protocol-like customer boundary, not a real recoverable objection.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to acknowledge the boundary explicitly ('understood, we would never need to touch your roof for a detached structure') rather than pivoting straight to a technical question about the pavilion's own roof.

quote: if I would have to do a pavilion and then at that point get in touch with you all?
stewart_read: The customer directly asks the sequencing question — build the pavilion first, then call ION back — and hands the rep an opening to route her to Ion's in-house structure-building or roofing capability. The rep's answer trails off unfinished.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed moment on the call: the customer is asking to be told what Ion can do to help her get from 'no pavilion' to 'ready for solar.' The rep should complete the thought and offer a concrete next step (e.g., can Ion's roofing/construction side help, or should she call back once built) instead of leaving the sentence hanging.

quote: Yeah. The structure would have to be built, but,
stewart_read: This is the last substantive rep line in the call and it's incomplete — no next step, no callback date, no confirmation of how she should re-engage. The customer is left to propose and close the call herself at 02:55.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read considered: rep may have been letting her finish her own thought before summarizing; rejected because no rep line follows to close the loop before the customer says goodbye.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to always land the call with an owned next step, even on an out-of-scope inquiry — e.g., 'call us back once the pavilion's built and we'll get you scheduled with a design specialist' stated plainly, not implied.

quote: So we can just get back in touch with you once a structure is built. Okay. And then we'll go from there.
stewart_read: The customer, not the rep, defines the resolution and closes the call. No day, time, or CRM-trackable follow-up exists — this is a full button-up miss.
coaching_implication: Have the rep review Ion's button-up checklist: even a non-standard, DQ-adjacent scenario like this should end with the rep restating the plan and, ideally, capturing a way to re-contact her (email/text) rather than letting her hang up on her own terms.

quote: So it would be on a on a structure near near the Okay. 25 feet, 50 feet of the home.
stewart_read: The customer is actively planning new construction (a pavilion) specifically to house solar — this is a build-it-for-solar intent signal, more qualified than a passive lead, but the rep never anchors on it or captures her timeline/budget for the structure.
coaching_implication: Manager should note: a customer proactively describing plans to build a structure just to add solar is a strong future-pipeline signal. Rep should have captured a rough timeline and offered a follow-up touchpoint instead of leaving it as 'get back in touch.'

quote: I don't have it. I don't even have the pavilion at this point. I just was there was an ad that went on there that showed a pavilion roof with solar panels, and I didn't know if that was something you guys did.
stewart_read: This call is fundamentally a non-standard scenario (no home rooftop install possible, no structure yet exists) that the standard verify/bill script doesn't cover. The rep never explicitly names this as an edge case or escalates/notes it for a supervisor or specialized routing.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep just didn't know how to handle it; strategic read (rejected) that he was intentionally deferring is not supported since no follow-up plan or escalation is captured anywhere in the transcript.
coaching_implication: Flag for training: reps need a defined path for 'no structure exists yet' inquiries — capture contact info and timeline, log as a future lead, rather than let the call fade out.
